title: II. The Duel
paragraphs: _(c) Recollections of Father Zossima’s Youth before he became a Monk. The Duel_

I spent a long time at the military cadet school in Petersburg, almost eight years. Everything there was new to me, and many of my childhood impressions grew fainter, though I forgot nothing. I picked up so many new habits and opinions that I turned into a cruel, absurd, almost savage creature. I did acquire a surface polish of courtesy and social manners, along with the French language.

But all of us, myself included, looked on the soldiers who served us as cattle. I was perhaps worse than the rest in this, because I was so much more impressionable than my companions. By the time we left the school as officers, we were ready to die for the honor of the regiment. Yet not one of us had any idea what honor really meant, and if anyone had known, he would have been the first to laugh at it. Drunkenness, debauchery and devilry were almost what we prided ourselves on. I do not say we were bad by nature. All these young men were good fellows, but they behaved badly, and I behaved worst of all. What made it worse for me was that I had come into my own money. So I threw myself into a life of pleasure and plunged headlong into all the recklessness of youth.

I was fond of reading, yet, strange to say, the Bible was the one book I never opened in those days. I always carried it with me and was never parted from it. In very truth I was keeping that book “for the day and the hour, for the month and the year,” though I did not know it.

After four years of this life, I happened to be in the town of K., where our regiment was stationed at the time. We found the townspeople hospitable, rich and fond of entertainment. I was welcomed warmly everywhere, because I had a lively temperament and was known to be well off, which always counts for a great deal in the world. And then something happened that was the beginning of it all.

I became attached to a beautiful and intelligent young girl, of noble and lofty character, the daughter of highly respected people. They were well-to-do, with influence and position, and they always received me warmly and kindly. I imagined that the young lady looked on me with favor, and my heart was on fire at the thought. Later I saw and fully understood that perhaps I was not so passionately in love with her at all. I only recognized the elevation of her mind and character, which I could hardly have failed to do. But my selfishness kept me from proposing at that time. I was reluctant to give up the pleasures of my free and licentious bachelor life, in the prime of my youth and with my pockets full of money. I did drop some hint of my feelings, but I put off any decisive step for a while. Then, all of a sudden, we were ordered away to another district for two months.

When I came back two months later, I found the young lady already married to a rich landowner of the neighborhood. He was a very amiable man, still young though older than I was, connected with the best Petersburg society, which I was not, and well educated, which I also was not. I was so overwhelmed by this unexpected blow that my mind was positively clouded. The worst of it was that, as I learned then, the young landowner had been engaged to her for a long time. I had met him many times in her house, but blinded by my conceit I had noticed nothing. And this mortified me most of all: almost everybody had known about it, while I knew nothing. I was filled with sudden, uncontrollable fury. My face burned as I recalled how often I had been on the point of declaring my love to her. She had not tried to stop me or warn me, so I concluded that she must have been laughing at me all the time. Later, of course, I thought it over and remembered that she had been very far from laughing at me. On the contrary, she used to turn aside any love-making of mine with a joke and start talking about other things. But at that moment I could not reflect, and I was all eagerness for revenge. I am surprised, remembering it, that my rage and vengefulness were so extremely repugnant to my own nature. I was easygoing and found it hard to stay angry with anyone for long. So I had to work myself up artificially, and I ended by becoming revolting and absurd.

I waited for an opportunity and managed to insult my “rival” in front of a large company. I insulted him over a perfectly unrelated matter, jeering at his opinion about an important public event—it was in the year 1826[5]—and my jeer was, so people said, clever and effective. Then I forced him to demand an explanation, and I behaved so rudely that he accepted my challenge, despite the great gap between us. I was younger, a nobody, and of lower rank. I learned afterwards, for a fact, that he accepted out of jealousy too. He had been rather jealous of me on his wife’s account before they married. Now he imagined that if he swallowed my insult and refused my challenge, and if she heard of it, she might begin to despise him, and her love for him might waver. I soon found a second in a comrade, an ensign of our regiment. In those days duels were severely punished, yet dueling was a kind of fashion among the officers—so strong and deeply rooted can a brutal prejudice sometimes be.

It was the end of June, and our meeting was set for seven o’clock the next day on the edge of town. And then something happened that was truly the turning point of my life. That evening I came home in a savage and brutal mood and flew into a rage with my orderly Afanasy. I hit him twice in the face with all my strength, so that it was covered with blood. He had not been long in my service, and I had struck him before, but never with such ferocious cruelty. And believe me, though it was forty years ago, I remember it now with shame and pain. I went to bed and slept for about three hours. When I woke, day was breaking. I got up—I did not want to sleep any more—I went to the window and opened it. It looked out on the garden. I saw the sun rising. It was warm and beautiful, and the birds were singing.

“What does this mean?” I thought. “Something in my heart feels vile and shameful. Is it because I am about to shed blood? No,” I thought, “that is not what it is. Can it be that I am afraid of death, afraid of being killed? No, not that, not that at all.”... And all at once I knew what it was: I had beaten Afanasy the evening before! It all rose up in my mind, it all happened again before my eyes. He stood in front of me while I beat him straight in the face. He held his arms stiffly at his sides, his head erect, his eyes fixed on me as though he were on parade. He staggered at every blow and did not even dare to raise a hand to protect himself. That is what a man had been brought to, and it was one man beating another! What a crime! It felt as if a sharp dagger had gone right through me. I stood as though struck dumb, while the sun shone, the leaves rejoiced and the birds trilled their praise of God.... I hid my face in my hands, fell on my bed and broke into a storm of tears. And then I remembered my brother Markel and what he said on his deathbed to his servants: “My dear ones, why do you wait on me, why do you love me, am I worth your waiting on me?”

“Yes, am I worth it?” the thought flashed through me. “What am I really worth, that another man, a fellow creature, made in the likeness and image of God, should serve me?” For the first time in my life this question forced itself on me. Markel had said, “Mother, my little heart, in truth we are each responsible to all for all. It is only that men do not know this. If they knew it, the world would be a paradise at once.”

“God, can that be false too?” I thought as I wept. “In truth, perhaps I am more responsible than anyone for everything, a greater sinner than any man in the world.” And all at once the whole truth stood before me in its full light. What was I about to do? I was about to kill a good, clever, noble man who had done me no wrong. By taking away his wife’s happiness for the rest of her life, I would be torturing and killing her too. I lay there on my bed with my face in the pillow, not noticing how the time was passing. Suddenly my second, the ensign, came in with the pistols to fetch me.
“Ah,” said he, “good, you’re up already. It’s time we left. Come on!”
I did not know what to do, and I hurried back and forth, unable to decide. Still, we went out to the carriage.
“Wait here a minute,” I told him. “I’ll be right back. I forgot my purse.”
And I ran back alone to Afanasy’s little room.
“Afanasy,” I said, “yesterday I hit you twice in the face. Forgive me.”

He gave a start, as if he were frightened, and stared at me. And I saw that this was not enough. Right there, in my full officer’s uniform, I dropped at his feet and touched my forehead to the ground.
“Forgive me,” I said.
Then he was utterly aghast.
“Your honor ... sir, what are you doing? Am I worth it?”
And he burst into tears, as I had done a little while before. He hid his face in his hands, turned to the window and shook all over with sobs. I flew out to my comrade and jumped into the carriage.
“Ready,” I cried. “Ever seen a conqueror?” I asked him. “Well, here’s one for you.”
I was in ecstasy, laughing and chattering all the way. I do not remember about what.
He looked me over. “Well, brother, you’re a plucky fellow. You’ll keep up the honor of the uniform, I can see.”

So we arrived and found the others already waiting for us. We were placed twelve paces apart, and he had the first shot. I stood there cheerfully and looked him full in the face. I did not so much as blink. I looked at him with love, for I knew what I was going to do. His bullet just grazed my cheek and ear.
“Thank God,” I cried, “nobody’s dead!” Then I seized my pistol, turned around and hurled it far into the wood. “That’s where you belong,” I cried.
I turned to my adversary.

“Forgive me, sir, for being a young fool,” I said. “I insulted you for no reason, and I made you fire at me. I am ten times worse than you, and more, maybe. Tell that to the person you hold dearest in the world.”
No sooner had I said this than all three of them started shouting at me.
“Good heavens,” cried my adversary, irritated, “if you didn’t want to fight, why couldn’t you have left me in peace?”
“Yesterday I was a fool. Today I’m wiser,” I answered him cheerfully.
“About yesterday I believe you, but about today I find it hard to agree,” said he.
“Bravo,” I cried, and clapped my hands. “I agree with you there as well. I deserved that!”
“Will you shoot, sir, or won’t you?”
“No, I won’t,” I said. “If you like, fire at me again, but you would do better not to.”
The seconds were shouting too, mine most of all: “Can you disgrace the regiment like this, facing your opponent and begging his pardon! If I had only known!”
I stood facing them all, no longer laughing.
“Gentlemen,” I said, “is it really so remarkable these days to meet a man who can repent of his stupidity and openly admit he was wrong?”
“Not in a duel!” my second cried again.

“That is just what is so strange,” I said. “I should have owned up the moment I arrived, before he fired a shot, before I led him into a great and deadly sin. But we have made our life so grotesque that behaving like that was almost impossible. My words could mean something to him only after I had stood his fire at twelve paces. If I had spoken earlier, he would have said, ‘He’s a coward, the sight of the pistols has scared him, it’s no use listening to him.’ Gentlemen,” I cried suddenly, speaking straight from my heart, “look around you at the gifts of God: the clear sky, the pure air, the tender grass, the birds. Nature is beautiful and sinless, and we, only we, are sinful and foolish. We do not understand that life is heaven. We have only to understand that, and heaven will at once be fulfilled in all its beauty. We shall embrace each other and weep.”
I would have said more, but I could not. My voice broke with the sweetness and youthful joy of it, and my heart was filled with a bliss I had never known before in my life.
“All very rational and edifying,” said my antagonist, “and you are certainly an original.”
“Laugh if you like,” I said, laughing too, “but later you will approve of me.”
“Oh, I can approve of you right now,” said he. “Will you shake hands? I believe you are perfectly sincere.”
“No,” I said, “not yet. Wait until I have become a better man and earned your respect. Then shake my hand, and you will do well.”
We went home, my second berating me the whole way while I kept kissing him. All my comrades heard of the affair at once, and that same day they gathered to sit in judgment on me.
“He has disgraced the uniform,” they said. “He should resign his commission.”
Some defended me: “He stood the shot,” they said.
“Yes, but he was afraid of the second one and begged for pardon.”

“If he had been afraid of getting shot, he would have fired his own pistol before asking pardon, rather than throwing it loaded into the forest. No, there is something else behind this, something original.”

I enjoyed listening to them and looking at them. “My dear friends and comrades,” said I, “do not trouble yourselves about my resigning, because I have already done it. I sent in my papers this morning, and as soon as I get my discharge I will enter a monastery. That is why I am leaving the regiment.”
As soon as I had said this, every one of them burst out laughing.
“You ought to have told us that first. That explains everything. We can’t judge a monk.”

They laughed and could not stop, and not scornfully but kindly and merrily. All at once they felt friendly toward me, even the ones who had condemned me most sternly. For the whole month until my discharge came, they made a great fuss of me. “Ah, you monk,” they would say. Everyone said something kind to me. They began trying to talk me out of it, even to pity me: “What are you doing to yourself?”
“No,” they would say, “he is a brave fellow. He stood fire, and he could have fired his own pistol too. But the night before, he dreamed he would become a monk, and that’s why he did it.”

It was the same with the society of the town. Until then I had been received kindly but had attracted no special attention. Now everyone got to know me at once, and everyone invited me. They laughed at me, but they loved me. I should mention that although everybody talked openly about our duel, the authorities paid it no mind. My antagonist was a close relation of our general, and since no blood had been shed and nothing serious had come of it, and since I had resigned my commission, they treated it as a joke. And from then on I began to speak out loud and without fear, regardless of their laughter, for their laughter was always kindly and never spiteful. These conversations mostly took place in the evenings, in the company of ladies. Women especially liked to hear me, and they made the men listen.
“But how can I possibly be responsible for everyone?” they would laugh in my face. “Am I, for instance, responsible for you?”

“It is no wonder you do not know it,” I would answer, “since the whole world has long been going a different way. We take the plainest lies for truth, and we demand the same lies from others. Here, for once in my life, I have acted sincerely, and, well, you all take me for a madman. You are friendly to me, but still, you see, you all laugh at me.”

“But how could we not be friendly to you?” said my hostess with a laugh. The room was full of people. Suddenly the young lady stood up, the one the duel had been fought over, the one I had lately meant to marry. I had not seen her come in. She rose, walked over to me and held out her hand.
“I want you to know,” she said, “that I am the first who does not laugh at you. I thank you with tears, and I respect you for what you did that day.”

Her husband came over too, and then they all gathered round me and very nearly kissed me. My heart was full of joy. But one man in particular caught my eye, a man of middle age who had come up with the rest. I knew his name already, yet I had never met him or spoken a word to him before that evening.
_(d) The Mysterious Visitor_

He had held office in our town for many years. His position was a prominent one, everyone respected him, he was rich, and he was known for his kindness. He gave large sums to the almshouse and the orphanage, and he was generous in secret as well, which only came out after he died. He was about fifty, almost stern in appearance, and he did not talk much. He had been married some ten years, and his wife, who was still young, had borne him three children. Well, the next evening I was sitting alone in my room when the door suddenly opened and in walked this gentleman.

I should say, by the way, that I no longer lived in my old lodgings. As soon as I left the army, I rented rooms from an old lady, the widow of a government clerk. Her servant waited on me. The reason I had moved into her house at all was that, coming back from the duel, I had sent Afanasy back to the regiment. After my last talk with him I was ashamed to look him in the face. That is how quick a worldly man is to feel shame at a righteous deed.

“For the last few days,” said my visitor, “I have listened to you with great interest as you spoke in various houses. At last I wanted to meet you in person, so that we might talk more freely. Would you grant me that favor, dear sir?”

“Gladly, with the greatest pleasure. I shall count it an honor.” I said it, though I felt almost dismayed, so deeply did this man impress me from the first moment. Others had listened to me with interest and attention, but nobody had ever come to me looking so serious, so stern and so intent. And now he had come to my own rooms. He sat down.
“I see that you have great strength of character,” he said. “You have dared to serve the truth, even at the risk of everyone’s contempt.”
“You may be praising me too highly,” I replied.

“No, not too highly,” he answered. “Believe me, what you did is much harder than you think. That is what struck me, and that is the only reason I have come to you,” he went on. “Tell me, please, if my curiosity, which may be improper, does not annoy you, what exactly did you feel, if you can remember, at the moment you decided to ask forgiveness at the duel? Do not take my question for an idle one. I have a private reason for asking, which I may explain later, if God wills that we come to know each other better.”
The whole time he spoke, I looked him straight in the face. All at once I felt complete trust in him, and I was very curious too, for I sensed that his soul held some strange secret.

“You ask what exactly I felt when I asked my opponent’s forgiveness,” I answered. “But I had better begin at the beginning, with something I have told no one yet.” And I told him everything that had passed between Afanasy and me, and how I had bowed down at his feet to the ground. “So you can see for yourself,” I concluded, “that at the duel it was easier for me. I had made a start already at home. Once I was on that road, going further along it was not hard at all. It became a source of joy and happiness.”
I liked the way he looked at me while he listened. “All of this,” he said, “is most interesting. I shall come and see you again and again.”

From then on he came to see me almost every evening. We could have become closer friends, if only he had ever spoken of himself. But of himself he said hardly a word, while he never stopped asking about me. Still, I grew very fond of him and talked to him quite openly about all I felt. “For why,” I thought, “should I need to know his secrets, when I can see without them that he is a good man? And grave as he is, and older than I, he still comes to see a youngster like me and treats me as an equal.” I learned a great deal of value from him, for he had a lofty mind.

“That life is heaven,” he said to me suddenly, “is a thought I have turned over for a long time.” Then he added all at once, “In fact, I think of nothing else.” He looked at me and smiled. “I am more sure of it than you are. I will tell you later why.”
I listened and thought that he clearly wanted to tell me something.
“Heaven,” he went on, “lies hidden in every one of us. It lies hidden in me now. If I choose, it will be revealed to me tomorrow and for all time.”
I looked at him. He spoke with deep feeling, and he gazed at me mysteriously, as if he were putting a question to me.

“As for our being all responsible to all and for all, over and above our own sins, you were quite right to think so. It is wonderful that you grasped its whole meaning at once. And truly, once men understand this, the Kingdom of Heaven will be no dream for them but a living reality.”
“And when?” I cried out bitterly. “When will that happen? Will it ever happen? Or is it only a dream of ours?”

“So you do not believe it?” he said. “You preach it and do not believe it yourself. Believe me, this dream, as you call it, will certainly come true. It will come, but not yet, for every process has its law. This is a spiritual, a psychological process. If the world is to be changed and made new, men must first turn to another path in their minds. Until you have truly, in actual fact, become a brother to everyone, brotherhood will not come. No scientific teaching, no common interest, will ever teach men to share property and privilege with the same fairness to all. Everyone will think his share too small. They will always be envying one another, complaining and attacking. You ask when it will come. It will come, but first we must pass through a time of isolation.”
“What do you mean by isolation?” I asked him.

“Why, the isolation that rules everywhere, most of all in our age. It is not yet fully grown. It has not yet reached its limit. Each man strives to hold his individuality as far apart as he can. Each wants the fullest possible life for himself. But all his efforts end not in a fuller life but in self-destruction, because instead of finding himself he ends in utter solitude. In our age all mankind has broken up into separate units. They all keep apart, each in his own rut. Each stands aloof, hiding himself and what he owns from the rest, and he ends by being pushed away by others and pushing them away. He piles up riches alone and thinks, ‘How strong I am now, how safe!’ In his madness he does not see that the more he piles up, the further he sinks into helplessness that destroys him. For he is used to trusting himself alone and to cutting himself off from the whole. He has trained himself not to believe in help from others, from men or from humanity, and he trembles only lest he lose his money and the privileges he has won. In these days, men in their mockery have stopped seeing, everywhere, that real safety lies in standing together with others, not in each one’s lonely effort. But this terrible individualism must come to an end, and suddenly all will see how unnaturally they have been parted from one another. It will be the spirit of the time, and people will be amazed that they sat so long in darkness without seeing the light. And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the heavens.... Until then, though, we must keep the banner flying. Sometimes, even if he must do it alone and even if he seems to be acting like a madman, a man has to set an example. He must draw other souls out of their loneliness and rouse them to some act of brotherly love, so that the great idea does not die.”

So our evenings went by, one after another, in this stirring and passionate talk. I gave up society and called on my neighbors far less often. My vogue, besides, was somewhat past. I do not say this to complain, for they still loved me and treated me kindly, but there is no denying that fashion is a mighty power in society. I came to look on my mysterious visitor with admiration. I enjoyed his intelligence, and I also began to see that he was brooding over some plan in his heart and perhaps preparing for a great deed. Perhaps he was pleased that I showed no curiosity about his secret and made no attempt to learn it, by direct question or by hints. But in the end I saw that he seemed to be showing signs of wanting to tell me something. About a month after his first visit this had become quite plain.
“Do you know,” he said to me once, “that the people in town are very inquisitive about us? They wonder why I visit you so often. Let them wonder, for _soon all will be explained_.”

At times a strange agitation would seize him, and nearly always he would then get up and leave. At times he would fix a long, piercing gaze on me, and I would think, “Now he is going to say something.” But he would abruptly start talking about some ordinary, familiar matter. He often complained of headaches too.
One day, with no warning at all, after he had been talking with great fervor for a long time, I saw him turn pale. His face twitched, and he stared hard at me.
“What is it?” I said. “Are you ill?” He had just been complaining of a headache.
“I ... you know ... I murdered someone.”
He said this and smiled, his face white as chalk. “Why is he smiling?” That thought flashed through my mind before I took in anything else. I turned pale too.
“What are you saying?” I cried.
“You see,” he said, with a pale smile, “what it has cost me to say the first word. Now it is said, I feel I have taken the first step, and I shall go on.”

For a long time I could not believe him. I did not believe him then, but only after he had come to me three days running and told me all of it. I thought he was mad, but I ended by being convinced, to my great grief and amazement. His crime was great and terrible.

Fourteen years earlier he had murdered a landowner’s widow, a rich and beautiful young woman who owned a house in our town. He fell passionately in love with her, told her so, and tried to persuade her to marry him. But she had already given her heart to another man, an officer of noble birth and high rank, who was away at the front at that time, though she expected him back soon. She refused his proposal and begged him to stop calling on her. After he had stopped, he used what he knew of the house to slip in one night through the garden and over the roof, at great risk of being caught. But, as often happens, a crime carried out with extraordinary boldness is more likely to succeed than others.

He climbed in through the skylight into the attic and went down the ladder. He knew the door at the foot of it was sometimes left unlocked, because the servants were careless. He hoped to find it so, and he did. In the dark he made his way to her bedroom, where a lamp was burning. As if on purpose, both her maids had gone off, without asking leave, to a birthday party in the same street. The other servants slept in their quarters or in the kitchen on the ground floor. The sight of her asleep set his passion blazing, and then spiteful, jealous rage seized his heart. Like a drunken man, out of his mind, he drove a knife into her heart, so that she did not even cry out. Then, with devilish and criminal cunning, he made sure that suspicion would fall on the servants. He was vile enough to take her purse, to open her chest with keys from under her pillow and take things out of it, doing all this the way some ignorant servant would, leaving valuable papers and taking only money. He took some of the larger gold objects but left smaller things worth ten times as much. He also took a few things for himself as keepsakes, but of that later. When he had done this dreadful deed, he went back the way he had come.

Neither the next day, when the alarm was raised, nor at any time later in his life, did anyone dream of suspecting him. Nobody even knew of his love for her, for he was always reserved and silent and had no friend to whom he would have opened his heart. People saw him merely as an acquaintance of the dead woman, and not a close one, since for the past two weeks he had not even called on her. Suspicion fell at once on one of her serfs, a man called Pyotr, and every circumstance bore it out. The man knew, and his mistress had not hidden it, that she had to send one of her serfs as a recruit and had decided on him, because he had no family and his behavior was poor. People had heard him threaten angrily, drunk in a tavern, to kill her. Two days before her death he had run away and was staying nobody knew where in the town. The day after the murder he was found on the road out of town, dead drunk, with a knife in his pocket, and by chance his right hand was stained with blood. He declared that he had had a nosebleed, but no one believed him. The maids admitted that they had gone to the party and that the street door had stood open until they got back. And a number of similar details came to light, all throwing suspicion on the innocent servant.

They arrested him and he was tried for the murder. But a week after his arrest the prisoner came down with a fever and died, unconscious, in the hospital. There the matter ended. The judges, the authorities and everyone in the town stayed convinced that the crime was the work of the servant who had died in the hospital, and no one else. And after that the punishment began.

My mysterious visitor, now my friend, told me that at first he felt no pangs of conscience whatever. He was wretched for a long time, but not for that reason. He only regretted that he had killed the woman he loved, that she was gone, that by killing her he had killed his love while the fire of passion was still in his veins. Of the innocent blood he had shed, of the murder of a fellow creature, he hardly thought. He could not bear the thought that she might have become another man’s wife, and so for a long time his conscience told him he could not have acted otherwise.

At first the servant’s arrest worried him, but the man’s illness and death soon set his mind at rest. As he reasoned at the time, the man had evidently died not of the arrest or the fright but of a chill caught on the day he ran away, when he lay all night on the damp ground, dead drunk. The theft of the money and other things troubled him little, for he argued that it had been done not for gain but to throw off suspicion. The sum was small, and soon afterwards he donated all of it, and much more, to the fund for keeping up an almshouse in the town. He did this deliberately, to quiet his conscience about the theft, and it is a remarkable fact that for a long time he really was at peace. He told me so himself. Then he threw himself into a career of great activity in the service. He volunteered for a hard and laborious duty that took up two years, and being a man of strong will, he almost forgot the past. Whenever it came back to him, he tried not to think of it at all. He became active in philanthropy as well. He founded and helped support many institutions in the town, did a good deal in the two capitals, and was elected a member of philanthropic societies in both Moscow and Petersburg.

In the end, though, he started brooding over the past, and the strain was more than he could bear. Then a fine, intelligent girl took his fancy, and soon afterward he married her. He hoped that marriage would lift his lonely gloom. He thought that if he began a new life and conscientiously did right by his wife and children, he would leave the old memories behind for good. The very opposite happened. Within the first month of the marriage he was being fretted all the time by one thought: “My wife loves me—but what if she knew?” When she first told him she would soon bear him a child, he was troubled. “I am giving life, but I have taken life.” Children came. “How dare I love them, teach and educate them? How can I talk to them of virtue? I have shed blood.” They were splendid children, and he longed to caress them. “But I can’t look at their innocent, candid faces. I am unworthy.”

Finally the blood of his murdered victim began to haunt him, bitterly and ominously: the young life he had destroyed, the blood that cried out for vengeance. He began to have awful dreams. But he was a man of fortitude, and for a long time he endured his suffering, thinking: “I shall expiate everything by this secret agony.” That hope too was in vain. The longer it went on, the worse his suffering grew.

Society respected him for his active benevolence, though his stern and gloomy character awed everyone. But the more he was respected, the less he could bear it. He confessed to me that he had thought of killing himself. Yet another idea began to haunt him, one he had at first dismissed as impossible and unthinkable, though in the end it gripped his heart so hard that he could not shake it off. He dreamed of standing up, going out and confessing before everyone that he had committed murder. For three years this dream had pursued him, taking different forms. At last he came to believe with his whole heart that if he confessed his crime, his soul would be healed and he would be at peace forever. But this belief filled him with terror, for how could he ever carry it out? And then came what happened at my duel.
“Looking at you, I have made up my mind.”
I looked at him.
“Is it possible,” I cried, clasping my hands, “that such a small thing could bring you to such a decision?”

“My decision has been growing for three years now,” he answered, “and what you told me only put the finishing touch on it. Looking at you, I blamed myself, and I envied you.” He said this almost sullenly.
“But no one will believe you,” I pointed out. “It was fourteen years ago.”
“I have proof, solid proof. I will show it.”
Then I wept and kissed him.

“Tell me one thing, just one thing,” he said, as though everything hung on me. “My wife, my children! My wife may die of grief. My children won’t lose their rank or property, but they’ll be a convict’s children, and forever! And what a memory, what a memory of me I shall leave in their hearts!”
I said nothing.
“And to be torn away from them, to leave them forever? It’s forever, you know, forever!”
I sat still and prayed silently. At last I got up, afraid.
“Well?” He looked at me.
“Go,” I said, “and confess. Everything passes; only the truth remains. When your children are grown, they will understand how noble your decision was.”

That time he left me looking like a man who had made up his mind. Yet for more than two weeks afterward he came to me every evening, still getting ready, still unable to bring himself to do it. He made my heart ache. One day he would arrive full of resolve and say with fervor:

“I know it will be heaven for me, heaven, the moment I confess. For fourteen years I’ve been in hell. I want to suffer. I will take my punishment and begin to live. You can go through the world doing wrong, but there’s no way back. Now I don’t dare love my neighbor, or even my own children. Good God, perhaps my children will understand what my punishment has cost me, and they won’t condemn me! God is not in strength but in truth.”
“Everyone will understand your sacrifice,” I told him. “If not at once, then later. For you have served truth, the higher truth, which is not of this earth.”
He would go away looking comforted. But the next day he would be back, bitter, pale and sarcastic.

“Every time I come, you look at me so inquisitively, as if to say, ‘He still hasn’t confessed!’ Wait a bit, and don’t despise me too much. It’s not as easy as you think. Maybe I won’t do it at all. You won’t go and inform on me, will you?”
Far from watching him with prying curiosity, I was afraid even to look at him. I was sick with anxiety, and my heart was full of tears. At night I could not sleep.

“I’ve just come from my wife,” he went on. “Do you know what the word ‘wife’ means? When I went out, the children called after me, ‘Good-by, father, hurry back and read _The Children’s Magazine_ with us.’ No, you can’t understand that! No one learns wisdom from another man’s woe.”
His eyes glittered and his lips twitched. Suddenly he brought his fist down on the table so hard that everything on it jumped. He had never done such a thing before; he was such a gentle man.

“But do I have to?” he cried. “Must I? No one has been condemned, no one has been sent to Siberia in my place. The man died of a fever. And I’ve been punished for the blood I shed by what I’ve suffered. Besides, I won’t be believed. They won’t believe my proofs. Do I need to confess? Do I? I’m ready to keep on suffering for the rest of my life for the blood I shed, if only my wife and children can be spared. Would it be just to drag them down with me? Aren’t we making a mistake? What is right in this case? And will people see it, will they appreciate it, will they respect it?”

“Good Lord!” I thought. “At a moment like this he is thinking of other people’s respect!” I felt so sorry for him that I believe I would have shared his fate if that could have comforted him. I saw he was beside himself. I was horrified, for I understood with my heart as well as my mind what such a decision meant.
“Decide my fate!” he cried again.

“Go and confess,” I whispered. My voice failed me, but I said it firmly. I picked up the New Testament from the table, the Russian translation, and showed him the Gospel of St. John, chapter 12, verse 24:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.”
I had been reading that very verse when he came in. He read it too.

“That’s true,” he said, but he smiled bitterly. “The things you find in those books are terrible,” he said after a pause. “It’s easy enough to push them at a person. And who wrote them? Can men really have written them?”
“The Holy Spirit wrote them,” I said.
“It’s easy for you to prattle on,” he said, smiling again, this time almost with hatred.
I took the book again, opened it somewhere else and showed him the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 10, verse 31. He read:
“It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”
He read it and simply threw the book down. He was shaking all over.

“A dreadful text,” he said. “I’ll admit you’ve picked fitting ones.” He got up from his chair. “Well!” he said. “Good-by. Perhaps I won’t come again ... we’ll meet in heaven. So for fourteen years I have been ‘in the hands of the living God.’ That is how one must think of those fourteen years. Tomorrow I will beg those hands to let me go.”
I wanted to take him in my arms and kiss him, but I did not dare. His face was twisted and dark. He left.

“Good God,” I thought, “what has he gone off to face!” I dropped to my knees before the ikon and wept for him before the Holy Mother of God, our swift defender and helper. I spent half an hour praying in tears. It was late, nearly midnight. Suddenly the door opened and he came in again. I was surprised.
“Where have you been?” I asked him.
“I think,” he said, “I’ve forgotten something ... my handkerchief, I think.... Well, even if I haven’t forgotten anything, let me stay a little.”
He sat down. I stood over him.
“You sit down too,” he said.
I sat. For two minutes we sat in silence. He looked at me intently and suddenly smiled (I remembered that), then stood up, embraced me warmly and kissed me.
“Remember how I came to you a second time,” he said. “Do you hear? Remember it!”
And he went out.
“Tomorrow,” I thought.

And so it was. I did not know that evening that the next day was his birthday. I had stayed in for the last few days, so I had had no chance to hear of it from anyone. Every year on that day he held a great gathering, and everyone in town came. This time was no different. After dinner he walked into the middle of the room holding a paper—a formal declaration addressed to the chief of his department, who was there. He read it aloud to the whole company. It gave a full account of the crime, in every detail.
“I cut myself off from men as a monster. God has visited me,” he said in conclusion. “I want to suffer for my sin!”

Then he took out all the things he had kept for fourteen years, which he thought would prove his crime, and laid them on the table. There were the murdered woman’s jewels, which he had stolen to turn suspicion away. There was a cross and a locket taken from her neck, with a portrait of her betrothed inside. There was her notebook, and two letters: one from her betrothed, telling her he would soon be with her, and her unfinished reply, left on the table to be sent next day. He had carried off those two letters—what for? Why had he kept them for fourteen years afterward, instead of destroying them as evidence against him?

And this is what happened. Everyone was amazed and horrified. No one would believe it, and they thought he had lost his wits, though they all listened with intense curiosity. A few days later every house had settled and agreed that the poor man was mad. The authorities could not refuse to take up the case, but they too let it drop. The trinkets and letters gave them pause, but they decided that even if these proved genuine, no charge could rest on them alone. Besides, she might have given him those things as a friend, or asked him to look after them for her. I heard afterward, though, that the murdered woman’s friends and relatives had proved the things were hers, and that there was no doubt about it. Yet nothing, in the end, was fated to come of it.

Five days later, everyone had heard that he was ill and in danger of dying. I cannot explain what his illness was; they said it was something with his heart. But word got out that his wife had talked the doctors into examining his state of mind as well, and that they had concluded he was insane. I gave nothing away, though people hurried to question me. And when I wanted to visit him, I was kept away for a long time, above all by his wife.

“You are the one who made him ill,” she told me. “He was always gloomy, but this past year people noticed he was strangely excited and did odd things. And now you have destroyed him. Your preaching has brought him to this. For the last month he was always with you.”

Indeed, not only his wife but the whole town was against me and blamed me. “It’s all your doing,” they said. I kept silent, and in fact I rejoiced in my heart, for I plainly saw God’s mercy toward a man who had turned on himself and punished himself. I could not believe he was insane.

At last they let me see him, since he insisted on saying good-by to me. I went in and saw at once that not only his days but his hours were numbered. He was weak and yellow, his hands shook, and he gasped for breath, but his face was full of tender, happy feeling.
“It is done!” he said. “I’ve been longing to see you for so long. Why didn’t you come?”
I did not tell him that they had refused to let me in.

“God has had pity on me and is calling me to Himself. I know I am dying, but for the first time in so many years I feel joy and peace. There was heaven in my heart from the moment I did what I had to do. Now I dare to love my children and kiss them. Neither my wife, nor the judges, nor anyone else has believed it. My children will never believe it either. I see God’s mercy to them in that. I shall die, and my name will be spotless for them. And now I feel God near. My heart rejoices as in Heaven ... I have done my duty.”
He could not go on. He gasped for breath and pressed my hand warmly, gazing at me with fervor. We did not talk for long, because his wife kept peeping in at us. But he had time to whisper to me:
“Do you remember how I came back to you that second time, at midnight? I told you to remember it. Do you know what I came back for? I came to kill you!”
I gave a start.

“When I left you, I went out into the darkness and wandered the streets, fighting with myself. And suddenly I hated you so much I could hardly stand it. He is all that binds me now, I thought, and he is my judge. I can’t refuse to face my punishment tomorrow, because he knows everything. It wasn’t that I was afraid you would betray me (I never even thought of that). I thought, ‘How can I look him in the face if I don’t confess?’ And if you had been at the other end of the earth, but alive, it would have made no difference. I could not bear the thought that you were alive, knowing everything and condemning me. I hated you as if you were the cause, as if you were to blame for it all. I came back to you then, remembering that there was a dagger lying on your table. I sat down and asked you to sit, and for a whole minute I turned it over in my mind. If I had killed you, that murder would have ruined me even if I had never confessed the other. But I didn’t think about that at all, and at that moment I didn’t want to. I only hated you and longed to take my revenge on you for everything. The Lord defeated the devil in my heart. But I tell you, you were never nearer death.”

A week later he died. The whole town followed him to the grave. The chief priest gave a speech full of feeling. Everyone mourned the terrible illness that had cut his life short. But after the funeral the whole town turned against me, and people even refused to see me. Some, at first a few and then more, did begin to believe his story. They came to me and questioned me with great interest and eagerness, for man loves to see the righteous brought down and disgraced. But I held my tongue, and very soon afterward I left the town. Five months later, by God’s grace, I set out on the safe and blessed path, praising the unseen finger that had guided me to it so clearly. And to this day I remember in my prayers the servant of God, Mihail, who suffered so greatly.
